title: Say’s Law in China
subtitle: Why China needs to produce much more output
contentHtml:

[In the late 2010s, I did a few posts complaining about our reckless fiscal policy. At the time, most internet pundits thought it was silly to worry about budget deficits, as interest rates were quite low. I pointed out that they would not be low forever. Now the problem is obvious, so I’ll refrain from commenting on the recent Scott Bessent clown show. (Stephen Kirchner has a good analysis, for interested readers.) I like to focus on areas where I might make a difference, where my views are outside the mainstream. In 2018, being a contrarian meant worrying about the danger of excessive budget deficits. Today, it means not worrying about China’s economy.]

I frequently run across articles insisting that China is producing too much. Here is a typical example, from Michael Froman at Foreign Affairs:

But when this latest surge plateaus or recedes, the game could well be up. It is difficult to identify a sector capable of generating another 30 percent of GDP growth for the Chinese economy. The property sector is in a prolonged downturn that could last for the better part of a generation. The infrastructure sector can no longer support new, unnecessary high-speed rail lines in third-tier cities. Manufacturing easily meets domestic demand. Services, which in most economies absorb displaced industrial labor, remain thin because the household share of consumption is too depressed to sustain them. The industries China could still develop—commercial aircraft, AI hardware—are too small to make up the difference.

Here is some data for per capita GDP (2026 estimates from the IMF):

US: $94,430 (both nominal and PPP)

Singapore: $107,758 (nominal) $173,708 (PPP)

Hong Kong $59,640 (nominal) $84,212 (PPP)

Taiwan $42,103 (nominal) $98,051 (PPP) [the CIA say $32,300. ̄\_(ツ)_/ ̄]

South Korea: $37,412 (nominal) $68,624 (PPP)

Japan: $35,703 (nominal) $59,207 (PPP)

China: $14,874 (nominal) $31,596 (PPP)

The PPP figures are clearly inaccurate, something I’ve complained about in other posts. I suspect that Japan and the four “tiger economies” have similar outputs, if measured correctly—say about $60,000 per capita GDP, PPP All five are well below US levels, and roughly double Chinese levels. If China wishes to catch up to these other East Asian countries, then it needs to roughly double its output and if it wishes to catch up to the US it needs to triple its output.

So why do pundits keep insisting that China is producing too much output? Is this like during the Great Depression when President Roosevelt suggested that the real problem was “overproduction"? Yes, it is a bit like that.

China’s per capita output is slightly above Mexico and Thailand and a bit below Argentina and Costa Rica. In my view, the Chinese should try to at least double their current per capita output. But how?

There are two primary ways to boost aggregate output. The easiest method is to print enough money to move from the current position to a position on the production possibilities curve. But that’s not likely to be a game changer—you can expect at best 5% to 10% more output, probably much less. Demand stimulus basically overcomes the sticky wage problem and soaks up the unemployed labor. But China’s main problem is that its labor simply isn’t very productive. To get a meaningful increase in output, you need to move the long run aggregate supply curve (LRAS) to the right, you need to expand the economy’s capacity to produce goods and services.

Don’t get me wrong, demand stimulus is certainly worth doing when NGDP is depressed, and I’d encourage the Chinese to adopt a monetary policy that is a bit more expansionary. But I very much doubt whether this would boost output by even 5%; it would still leave China much poorer than its neighbors.

So that leaves supply-side reforms. China needs to increase its production potential, its capacity to produce goods and services. There are basically two ways of doing this. First, China could keep its current economic system in place and invest a higher share of its GDP. Second, China could do structural reforms to make its economy more efficient, so that existing resources are used more productively.

The majority of pundits seem to believe that China is investing too much. I’m not sure that is true, but I agree with those who worry that much of the current investment is on projects with dubious benefits. Simply adding more investment is unlikely to solve China’s low output problem.

If demand stimulus is not enough, and if more investment is likely to produce disappointing returns, then that leaves only one meaningful option for growth—economic reforms. And there’s really only one recipe for growth that has proved robust—a regime of free markets with reasonable taxes and secure property rights.

Let’s look at the level of economic freedom in the US and the major East Asian economies. I used the Fraser ranking, as the Heritage ranking excludes Hong Kong. But I also put each economy’s position in the Heritage ranking in parentheses for comparison:

#5 United States (#22)

#38 South Korea (#19)

These rankings are subjective, as the Fraser and Heritage indices use somewhat different criteria. But one thing is clear, mainland China is far less free market than the other countries listed above in any plausible index.

In the past, China grew rapidly whenever it enacted reforms that made its economy at least slightly more capitalist. To join the ranks of the world’s richest economies, China needs to make its economy freer—more like Singapore, Taiwan and Hong Kong. Note that those three economies are composed mostly of ethnic Chinese, so there is no obviously cultural barrier to the mainland China achieving a similar level of success.

I suppose you could argue that there was some sort of selection bias in terms of who migrated to Singapore, Taiwan and Hong Kong, and that those places have people with above average human capital. But that argument doesn’t apply to Japan and South Korea, where living standards are at a similar level. China can and should do much better than its current level of per capita output. It needs to produce far more goods and services.

Someone who has real world experience investing in China might assume that I don’t know what I’m talking about. They might have found Chinese workers to be highly productive. But in a weird way that sort of proves my point. If at an individual level Chinese workers seem competent and hard-working, and yet China’s average labor productivity remains at a fairly low level—similar to Latin America—that means their talented workers are not being used to their best advantage. The whole point of free market reforms is to unlock the latent potential of China’s vast workforce. Anyone who visits China almost immediately encounters lots of workers doing make work jobs, such as aimlessly pushing a broom along the gutter of a Chinese street.

Now let’s go back to the quote at the beginning of this post. What are we to make of this:

It is difficult to identify a sector capable of generating another 30 percent of GDP growth for the Chinese economy.

China would need to increase its GDP by 100% to catch up to East Asia, and 200% to catch up to the US. Are there sectors capable of producing much more than they currently produce? If not, then that would presumably reflect supply side problems, a lack of productive capacity. But if you read Froman’s (pessimistic) analysis, you get the impression that demand is the biggest problem:

The property sector is in a prolonged downturn that could last for the better part of a generation. The infrastructure sector can no longer support new, unnecessary high-speed rail lines in third-tier cities. Manufacturing easily meets domestic demand. Services, which in most economies absorb displaced industrial labor, remain thin because the household share of consumption is too depressed to sustain them.

Again, aggregate demand is a problem, but it explains only a small fraction of China’s vast shortfall relative to the rest of East Asia, and the even larger shortfall relative to the US.

Say’s Law has been widely criticized because it is seen as somehow denying the existence of demand shortfalls. But even Jean-Baptiste Say understood that with sticky wages you could have temporary periods of unemployment, called a “glut”. Nonetheless, Say Law does tell us something very useful. Over any significant period of time, a country can “afford” what it can produce. So don’t tell me that the Chinese cannot afford to buy more stuff.

If there are sticky wages, then a country may temporarily produce less than its potential. But that would not be because Say’s Law is wrong, it would reflect the fact that sticky wages produce a gap between current output and potential. This problem can be easily resolved by printing more money. No country should ever refrain from boosting its output because of a worry that people won’t be able to “afford” the extra output.

Although China would do well to vastly increase its aggregate production of goods, there can be cases of too much production of some goods and too little of other goods, For instance, we continually hear about “overproduction” in the Chinese auto and housing industries. But what is the per capita ownership of cars in China? What is China’s per capita housing stock?

AI Overview says China has 330 cars per 1000 people, while Japan has about 600 per 1000 and the US has about 800 cars per 1000 people. In what sense does China not “need” more cars? China’s housing is about 650 square feet on average, compared to 2200 square feet in the US. The truth is that if China is to become a fully developed country it will need more of almost everything, including cars and housing. Overproduction is not China’s problem.

The Economist has a particularly egregious example of how pundits misjudge the Chinese economy.

In a lengthy new paper, the [Chinese] commerce ministry seeks to rebut the accusations of industrial excess levelled against China by many foreign governments and economists.

The paper is both rigorous and disingenuous. Some parts bring healthy scrutiny to the concept of overcapacity. The deep insincerity of other sections suggests contempt for countries facing waves of Chinese exports. . . .

Certainly, Chinese companies are low-cost producers, but that is no random market outcome, for the government has helped bring it about. . . .

The ministry’s discussion of state subsidies makes an art of dissimulation. It limits analysis only to direct subsidies—merely the most superficial of the techniques that China uses to favour its own companies. Other crucial forms of support include public investment in chipmakers, cheap land and rules compelling state firms to buy domestically. In the background are the policy settings—above all, a weak social safety-net—that have engendered a perpetually high savings rate. . . .

Foreign companies, however big, stand little chance against a Leninist developmental state that has attained China’s size, wealth and modernity. As Rhodium Group, an American research firm, points out, the Chinese state once limited its intervention to a handful of sectors that it deemed to be strategic; now it pursues an “industrial policy of everything”.

The phrase “contempt for countries facing waves of Chinese exports” seems to equate Chinese exports with a military invasion. Is that true? Are western consumers forced to buy Chinese EVs at gunpoint? Or are these voluntary transactions between consenting adults? I expect more from The Economist, which was founded in 1843 as a voice of reason in the free trade debate. Let’s review a few of the problems with their arguments:

  1. China is not special in either trade or manufacturing. As I showed in the previous post, its current account surplus is relatively small on a per capita basis, roughly 1/10th the level of the smaller East Asian and northern European economies. Pundits forget that China has about as many people as Europe, the US, Canada, Mexico, Japan and Australia combined. Of course it has a big manufacturing sector. Why wouldn’t it?

  2. Subsidies that boost output in some industries come at the expense of output in other industries. Contra The Economist, there is no such thing as an “industrial policy of everything”. Just as you cannot raise yourself by your bootstraps, you cannot boost aggregate output through subsidies. Indeed, subsidies generally tend to reduce aggregate output by making an economy less efficient than a more free market regime. China would produce more if it subsidized less.

  3. Government subsidies increase the budget deficit. Other things equal, this reduces domestic saving and thus reduces the current account surplus. China’s trade surplus is certainly not caused by government subsidies. Other East Asian countries have far bigger surpluses in per capita terms.

  4. Even if subsidies did help China to grow, why would this be a problem for the rest of the world? The only argument that I’ve ever heard that is even logical is the so-called predatory pricing argument—the claim that subsidies are a scheme to monopolize and then later raise prices sharply. But predatory pricing is about the last thing we should fear from China’s ultra-competitive economy. Indeed, the standard argument is that Chinese industries are too competitive to earn decent profits, which explains why their stock market does so poorly.

  5. And what are we to make of this claim?

Foreign companies, however big, stand little chance against a Leninist developmental state that has attained China’s size, wealth and modernity.

If China’s “size” is the issue, would the problem go away if China split up into 30 smaller countries? If “modernity” is the problem, would the world be better off if China remained an ancient kingdom? And why would China being “wealthy” be a problem? Indeed, in what sense is China wealthy? (Certainly not per capita.)

In a recent China Talk post Jordan Schneider, Irene Zhang, and Phoebe Chow point out that China is far from being a “Leninist developmental state”:

How did China grow its EV industry? Hint: it wasn’t really central planning from Beijing. It was a magical concoction of entrepreneurs and local officials using their guanxi to dance around giant SOEs and central-government regulation, leverage private and foreign capital, and just be really excellent business people. That’s led to our situation in 2026 — world-beating companies that have a ton of overcapacity and are set to take over the planet.

I cannot imagine anyone visiting Shanghai or Shenzhen and thinking, “This is sort of like the Soviet Union.” In any case, the Soviet Union was not a competitive threat to the West.

  1. And how about the claim that:

    “In the background are the policy settings—above all, a weak social safety-net—that have engendered a perpetually high savings rate.”

Northern Europe has the world’s most extensive social safety net, and yet those countries have high saving rates and run large current account surpluses.

Western pundits might envy China’s success, but how many would like to change places with a country at one half of Japan’s productivity and one third the US level? Pundits tell us that subsidies and trade surpluses explain China’s success, but exactly how much success does China actually have? Its economy has grown enormously since 1980, but from an extremely low base. Let’s hope it continues growing rapidly.

So, what should China do to boost economic growth? (K.I.S.S.)

  1. Free markets and stronger property rights: I’m not going to suggest that China should do no industrial policy at all—even highly successful economies like Singapore, Hong Kong and the US have some industrial polices. China may wish to encourage green industries through a carbon tax. They may wish to promote a chip making industry for national security reasons. Rather I would argue that they should radically reduce their current level of industrial policy, by at least 90%. Eliminate most subsidies. Remove restrictions on internal migration. Privatize SOEs. Move toward freer trade and investment. Remove capital controls. Etc.

  2. Adopt NGDP targeting, level targeting, to make Says Law effective in the short run. (It already applies in the long run.)

The best way to think about complex macroeconomic issues is to keep a few basic principles in mind:

  1. Imports are good. Exports are the (unfortunate) price we pay for the imports we desire.

  2. Trade imbalances are not a problem.

  3. Subsidies don’t boost aggregate output, nor do they explain a country’s success in exporting.

  4. Excessive aggregate output is not a problem. The public can “afford” what it can produce.

  5. Because of sticky wages, NGDP instability can temporarily reduce output below potential. Eventually, the economy self-corrects. Persistently low output is generally caused by supply problems.

  6. China is extremely large. Otherwise, it is a completely normal middle-income country. The world should not fear it doubling or even tripling its aggregate output.

  7. Free market economies are usually richer than more statist economies.

In the media, China is portrayed as a sort of monstrous freak that threatens the world economy. Don’t believe the hype. Textbook economics circa 1999 is still true.
